title: The work list
dek: What is being done here, as opposed to what is known.
lead: This archive already had five registers for what it knows — the open questions, the research log, the sources, the method, and the corrections folded into each page. It had none for what it is doing. That lived in a chat window, which is the one place that does not survive the session, and on 15 September it cost a letter sent to a woman who had been thanked fourteen hours earlier. This is the register that answers who has to move next.
close: Everything here owned by David is a decision or a payment. Everything owned by this archive is work that can start without asking anybody. Everything blocked is waiting on a filing cabinet in South Africa, Portugal, Poland or Germany — or on one of five living people who were written to about a finding that concerns them.

rows.what: Confirm Leonard Aubrey Robert Wear as Derrick's biological father from a document, not an inference
rows.note: The DNA proves Derrick descends from **Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle as a couple** — 253 of the 297.5 cM he shares with his closest match lie outside every region he shares with any Castle cousin. The couple had **two sons**, and in June 1948 one was thirty-one and the other was eleven. What is missing is a record naming Leonard as anybody's father. Two death notices were requested from the Master at Cape Town on 15 September; see [the DNA page](/dna/).

rows.what: Master of the High Court, Cape Town — J294 death notices in estates 10761/2024 and 018561/2021
rows.note: Gillian Agnes Louisa Nel, born Wear, and Patricia Mary Maud Grant, born Wear. Each file holds a death notice with a field for the **father's full names**. Sent to Mr D Keyster, the estate controller for file numbers ending in 1. His auto-reply diverts only appointment queries, so a copy request should stay with him. Ms N Mphetshwa has left the section — that cc was wasted, and on 15 September her own auto-reply CONFIRMED it in her own words: "kindly note that I am no longer working at the Deceased Estate Appointment section". Mr Keyster's auto-reply also fired and diverts APPOINTMENT queries only, to Ms Portia Arendse — so a copy request correctly stays with him. Both confirmations, neither an answer. VINDICATED 15 September by row 33: six marriage registers across thirty years and two form designs have been read and NONE records a parent. The J294 death notice asks for the father's full names and the mother's maiden name, which makes this letter the best South African route to the one fact the archive cannot document — not a redundant one. ANSWERED 15 September at 09:57 — the first substantive reply on this row. Mr Keyster asks for a formal application on an attached form, APPLICATION FORM FOR COPIES.pdf, with proof of payment, submitted 'on groundfloor' at 45 Castle Street, Dullah Omar Building, Cape Town. That last part is an IN-PERSON instruction and David is in Australia — but Mr Keyster answered by email, so email submission may well be acceptable and must be asked rather than assumed. His reply also gives neither the fee nor the banking details, and nothing can be paid without them. A reply is drafted asking exactly those two things. The form itself is a PDF attachment this archive cannot open, so David has to read it. Replied the same hour, Gmail 1a0a482ea47212a0, asking the two questions and — deliberately — restating that David is not a relative and claims no interest in either estate, so that if his office limits copies to interested parties the refusal arrives before the money does.

rows.what: National Archives, Pretoria — four Luwinski court files, 1948 to 1951
rows.note: **WLD 2545/1950 — IVONE versus KURT, restitution of conjugal rights.** She sued him. That is the step a deserted spouse takes, and it sits between the divorce he filed in 1948 (**WLD 1950/1948**) and the one he filed in 1951 (**497/1951** and **2368/1951**). Four actions in three years, in both directions, with Derrick born in the middle of them. It hid because NAAIRS spells both names wrong — *Luwenski*, *Figaretto* — so every sweep missed it twice over. Sent to `Enquiries2@dsac.gov.za`, with 2545/1950 named as the one to do first.

rows.what: Henry Robert Wear's own estate, MHG 10245/69 — its death notice names his children
rows.note: This would test the whole Letchworth reconstruction against a South African record rather than an English index. **It cannot be emailed**: Ms Mavis Xaba of the Reading Room confirmed on 14 September that MHG files are *bound* and cannot be scanned. Added on 15 September to the commission the Lerena/Booyzen session already placed with a private researcher — same depot, same visit, and flagged as the least important of the seven.

rows.what: The two ante-nuptial contracts, June 1948 and February 1956
rows.note: Both marriages are recorded on the civil registers as entered into **WITH** an antenuptial contract, so the deeds exist. They sit in a **Deeds Registry**, which is a different institution from the archives and will not act on a letter or a telephone call. Stuck for weeks; on 15 September the researcher was asked whether she does that work or can name someone who does. AMENDED 15 September: there are THREE, not two. The Wear-Dunlop contract of 30 October 1951 was found the same evening by reading certificate 1397 at full resolution, and it is the only one of the three that names Leonard. Request 18 carries the correction and is held until the researcher replies.

rows.what: Four letters to living DNA matches, and one to a stranger about her own father
rows.note: Three went into threads opened in June 2025. The fourth — to the keeper of the seven-person tree that is the only source giving Leonard a mother called Castle — was **the first cold approach this archive has made**, and it tells a stranger that her father probably had a son she has never heard of. It also went to an account belonging to a woman who **died in March 2024**, so it may be read by her family or by nobody.

rows.what: GenDatabase — permission to publish six facts that came from them and nowhere else
rows.note: Their terms forbid republishing without written permission and this archive is on the open web. Submitted 15 September. **If refused**, those six facts come off the public pages into the working notes and the site will say a source asked for them to go, rather than deleting them quietly. It costs the argument nothing — the Wear reconstruction rests on English indexes and the Government Gazette, neither of which is theirs.

rows.what: Eleven institutional letters still unanswered — Berlin, Bydgoszcz, Koszalin, Maputo, Porto, Lisbon, Pretoria, Johannesburg
rows.owner: eight archives and two Masters' offices
rows.note: Two acknowledged: the Arquivo Histórico Militar in nine minutes, and Bydgoszcz with a warning that a complicated query can take over a month. Everything else is silence. See [the status page](/status/).

rows.what: Read the 1948 Johannesburg marriage register at full resolution
rows.note: Done 15 September. Read a third time, and this time from the archive's own microfilm rather than from a photograph in the family tree: digital film 008109682, frame 2047, image ark 3:1:3Q9M-CSJ1-SJQK. FamilySearch's own pages would not render — the session had been rate-limited to about one response every thirty-five seconds, which the site's front end shows as a hang — so the page was rebuilt locally from its 108 deep-zoom tiles and every cell magnified between four and five times, with the sideways columns rotated upright. One real correction: the couple's address is 108 DUNOTTAR Street, SYDENHAM, not Dunstan Street, Braamfontein. Everything the argument rests on holds, including the one that matters — column (10) reads With A.N.C. at 5.2x, four letters, not Without.

rows.what: Settle whether Leonard died in 1973 or 1979
rows.note: Worked hard on 15 September and not settled — but the evidence is now correctly weighed, which it was not before. Three routes failed. NAAIRS is down a second day, returning "The connection to the Search Manager Server is inactive" with an empty database list. Gazettes.Africa returns nothing for "Leonard Aubrey Robert Wear", "Wear, Leonard" or "L. A. R. Wear" in any year — and that proves nothing, because the control damns it: a search for Luwinski returns eight documents and not one is Kurt's own 1969 estate notice, which certainly existed. FamilySearch has both his marriages and no death record at all. What did change: GenDatabase's own profile page says in its own words that this record is INCOMPLETE as per their verification, and prints his date of birth as the corrupt string 0017. So 1979 is a damaged entry in a state index and 1973 is a daughter's family tree, and neither is a document. The archive should stop preferring 1979. The cheap way to close it is GenDatabase's single Verified Report at R20, which releases the identity number, the place of death and the full date — a purchase, so it is David's to make and not this archive's. NARROWED 15 September: he was alive on 13 SEPTEMBER 1969, buying his father's grave at West Park. That rules out nothing — both 1973 and 1979 are after it — but it is a hard floor, from a municipal record. || SHARPENED DECISIVELY 16 September. Four instruments have now looked: the NAAIRS estate index (South Africa to end 1976) has no Wear estate 1970-1976; the Johannesburg cemetery registers hold six Wears and none is him; the GRO death index for England and Wales 1970-1985, >99% complete and printing DATES OF BIRTH, holds 241 Wears and none is him; and the GRO consular registers structurally cannot contain a South African death of either year. SO THERE IS EXACTLY ONE PLACE IN THE WORLD WHERE THIS DEATH CAN BE RECORDED: THE SOUTH AFRICAN DEATH REGISTER AT THE DEPARTMENT OF HOME AFFAIRS — and GenDatabase's 1979 entry is a transcription of precisely that register. That changes its standing entirely. It is not one disputed source among several; IT IS THE ONLY SOURCE THAT COULD EXIST, and the family tree's 1973 has now failed three separate tests and has nothing left to stand on. The archive still cannot SAY he died in 1979 — a corrupt transcription is a corrupt transcription — but it now knows exactly what to ask for and of whom: ONE DEATH-REGISTER ENTRY AT HOME AFFAIRS, PRETORIA.

rows.what: Find whether Bruce Wallace Wear had sons — a Y test from one would end this in a single reading
rows.note: **Not reachable from the sources available, and kept here so nobody tries it again the same way.** A son of Bruce born in the 1960s would be in his sixties now, so he is not in a *death* database; and South African civil marriages on FamilySearch stop at **1974**, so a marriage in the 1980s or 1990s is not there either. GenDatabase cannot find living people. **The Y-test route needs contact with living Wears, not records** — which makes it a question for the people already written to, not a search. **Retested 15 September at the family's push**, by the one route left — Michelle Ann Wear, b.1978, d.2017 Johannesburg, whose estate would name her parents. **She is in no gazette and not in GenDatabase at all.** Two routes, both closed.

rows.what: Date the Wear family's emigration
rows.note: **Answered: they were gone before 29 September 1939.** The 1939 Register has seven Wears in Hertfordshire and the household is not among them, and a national search returns Henry Robert Wear in the 1891, 1901, 1911 and 1921 censuses and then stops. The absence is real rather than redaction — born 1889 and 1895, he and Martha would be 137 and 131, so their records would be open if they existed. **One daughter stayed**: *Jeannett (E M) Wear, 1919, 18 Ridge Avenue, Letchworth*, aged twenty on register night. She followed later and died in South Africa in 2001.

rows.what: Re-run every woman in the archive by maiden name
rows.note: **Run, and the useful answer is a negative.** Ivone is in **no South African death record under any name she used** — not Salkow, not Luwinski, not de Witt, not Figueiredo, and no Ivone among the six women in the verified deaths carrying that maiden name. She married three times in that country and died out of its reach. **That is what dying in Porto looks like from this side**, and it is the first corroboration this archive has for a death it has never been able to date.

rows.what: Big Y-700 on Derrick's kit
rows.note: A purchase, and **this archive does not spend other people's money.** It would place him on a branch young enough for a surname to mean something. Of the 7,748 public members of the R-U106 project only 34 sit under R-S11477, whose common ancestor lived around 200 BCE — so the surnames on that branch are ninety generations away and mean nothing at all. SHARPENED 15 September by row 45. The argument for the Big Y is no longer 'more detail'. The classic haplotree shows forty-two branches below R-S11477, and its two immediate children are R-Z27559 and R-BY42072 — and R-BY42072 is TAGGED ENGLAND, as is R-FT370170 below it (13 testers, c. 550 CE). The Y evidence has so far only been able to say NOT ASHKENAZI. A Big Y that landed Derrick on one of those two branches would make it say something positive and geographically pointed for the first time.

rows.what: Whether Derrick should be told before any more strangers are
rows.note: Raised twice and overruled twice, which is the family's decision and not this archive's to make — but it is recorded here because it is still live. Five living people have now been written to about a finding that concerns a man who has not, so far as this archive knows, been told that his family is writing to them.

rows.what: Two archives share one mailbox, and neither knew what the other had sent
rows.note: The cause of the duplicate letter. `Projects/SHARED-CONTACTS.md` now sits in **both** this archive's notes and the Lerena/Booyzen one, listing every shared contact and its live state, every address known to be dead and why, and the constraints that apply to both. One rule at the top: **before writing to any institution, search the sent mail.**

rows.what: Track what comes back, not only what goes out
rows.note: The tracker recorded what was *sent* and never what was *said back*, so Ms Xaba's reply — that MHG files are bound and cannot be emailed — sat unread for a day while this archive went on framing every estate request as *just send me the one page*. There is now a **What has actually come back** table on [the status page](/status/).

rows.what: Order Edwina Ann Wear's estate, 33157/2014, for the parents named in its death notice
rows.note: **Founded on a mistake, and kept here rather than deleted.** A full day went into Edwina as Derrick's possible half-sister. She was born **Edwina Ann GREEN** and married Bruce Wallace Wear — Leonard's younger brother — in 1980. A Wear by marriage, no blood relation at all. Every dead end around her had been the answer saying so: her parents were unfindable under Wear because they were Greens, and she was still a Wear at 69 because it was her married name.

rows.what: Find the Halsey marriage that joins the Brown and Castle families to the surname on the closest match's card
rows.note: **Founded on a mistake.** A week went into the surname *Halsey* because it was the name printed on a DNA match card. It was the wrong half of a married couple: the 1952 register gives the birthplaces as **Cape Province** for him and **ENGLAND** for her, and the English link was the wife. There was never a Halsey marriage to find, which is exactly why the England and Wales index came back empty.

rows.what: Correct the archive's own errors in public rather than editing them away
rows.note: Standing work, and the reason this archive is worth anything. Published corrections to date: the Castles were **Hertfordshire, not Norfolk**; Caroline was a **Wallis**, not a Walls, and the tree was right where this archive was wrong; Derrick's birth year leaked onto the DNA page and was removed; the generation claim was walked back within the hour; and Henrique was called the son of a marriage that the 1948 register proves never happened. *** BROUGHT UP TO DATE 17 SEPTEMBER. *** The research log had stopped at 15 September while the archive went on making mistakes. NINE ENTRIES ADDED, of which SEVEN ARE MARKED WITHDRAWN OR CORRECTED: reading a dead hostname as a dead service; publishing two archive-index zeroes that were three records each; claiming DNA above George William Castle on a surname without opening the tree; having the emigration backwards, with the father leaving first; LEAKING THREE LIVING MATCH HOLDERS INTO A BUILD BECAUSE THE GUARD THAT CATCHES IT WAS NEVER WIRED INTO THE BUILD CHAIN; the Martha Giddings quarters; and the WALLIS/Walls contradiction that had sat on a page for a fortnight. The two genuine finds of the same days — Caroline James and Pix Road — sit in the same list in the same voice, which is the point of keeping it.

rows.what: Mervin Halsey's parents — the Henry George Charles and Mary Ellen guess
rows.note: **Founded on two birth years and killed by a third date.** This archive proposed Henry George Charles Halsey (1906–1993) and Mary Ellen Halsey (d.1981) as Mervin's parents because they were the right ages. But **he married Evelyn Ruth in 1932** and **Mervin was born on 15 June 1930** — two years earlier; Mary Ellen has no spouse recorded and is not his wife; and Mervin was born in the **Cape Province**, which nothing places any of them in. Off the critical path regardless: the Halsey line stopped mattering the moment column four of the 1952 register was read.

rows.what: What is filed behind marriage entry 858 of 1948 — and the back of the sheet
rows.note: Drafted as request 15 and DELIBERATELY NOT SENT. The plan was a letter to Home Affairs. Searching the sent mail first — the rule written after the Xaba duplication — turned up a reply from a professional South African researcher in May 2020 saying that certificates of any kind, abridged, unabridged or vault, can only be applied for IN PERSON at Home Affairs, that third-party applications are no longer accepted, and that an applicant living overseas must go through the South African Embassy or Consulate in their country. So the letter as conceived would have gone to an address that cannot act on it — the fourth dead address of this project, avoided this time before sending rather than after a bounce. It is redrafted to the High Commission in Canberra and asks HOW rather than asking for the record. And it surfaces something uncomfortable: if eligibility really is limited to immediate family, then for the 1948 marriage that means the two spouses, both long dead, and their son of record. This document cannot be got without Derrick, which collides with row 15. Raised once, here, and left with David.

rows.what: The reverse of the 1948 marriage register — the form says P.T.O. and nobody has turned it over
rows.note: Struck 15 September, with an answer rather than a shrug. The film viewer loaded once the throttle eased, and the frames either side of ours were opened: frame 2046 is certificate 764, Louw and Swanepoel; frame 2048 is certificate 295, Mowbray and Gemmer. Both are certificate FRONTS, both 19 June 1948. The film runs front, front, front across its 3,228 images. So the reverse of the sheet was never photographed, and no amount of patience with FamilySearch will produce it. The question is not dropped — it is folded into row 22, because the letter to Home Affairs about entry 858 has to ask for both sides of it now.

rows.what: The Wear–Dunlop ante-nuptial contract, Johannesburg, October 1951
rows.note: Found tonight by reading the register of Leonard's second marriage at full resolution: certificate 1397 of 1951, column 10, reads "with". So a notarial ante-nuptial contract was executed for Leonard Aubrey Robert Wear and Marjorie Eileen Dunlop, born Walker, and registered in the Johannesburg Deeds Office. This is the third ANC on the archive's list, after Kurt's two, and it is the only one of the three that names LEONARD. An ANC recites each party's full particulars and is not confined to the register's eleven columns, which makes it the best document about him this archive has ever had a route to. Goes to the Pretoria researcher with rows 4 and 5.

rows.what: Leonard's Second World War service record — SANDF Documentation Centre, Pretoria
rows.note: New tonight, from the 1940 marriage register: Leonard's occupation is entered as ARMY and his residence as ROBERTS HEIGHTS, PRETORIA — the Union Defence Force's principal base — on 7 September 1940, one year and one day after South Africa entered the war. Second World War service records are held by the SANDF Documentation Centre in Pretoria, and an attestation form gives full name, date and place of birth, next of kin and in most cases THE NAMES OF THE PARENTS. That is exactly what the archive is missing. The entire chain rests on Leonard being a son of Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle, and the only source saying so is a seven-person tree built by his daughter. An attestation form would turn that into a government record. SENT as request 16. Three things settled first. This mailbox already has an unanswered enquiry from David, sent 9 September for the sibling archive about the Booyzen family, so the draft opens by naming it — two cold letters in six days is how the Xaba duplication happened. The address the whole internet gives, sandfdoc@mweb.co.za, is DEAD: it bounced on 9 September with Relay access denied, and the Centre has moved from Visagie Street to Irene; archive@dod.mil.za is the live one. And he was almost certainly NOT an officer — officers were gazetted by full name, the control searches return their entries, and Leonard returns nothing under six spellings — so the letter asks for an attestation and a medal-roll entry rather than a commission. SENT 15 September to archive@dod.mil.za, Gmail 1a0a3b70c6389154. *** UNBLOCKED 16 SEPTEMBER: THERE IS NOW A SERVICE NUMBER TO QUOTE. *** 141272, Corporal, South Africa Union Defence Forces, from the War Office prisoner-of-war lists WO 392/15 and WO 392/21. This row has sat blocked because SANDF cannot search on a name and a guess. A NUMBER IS EXACTLY WHAT THEY CAN SEARCH ON. The request should also say he was a PRISONER OF WAR in Germany, listed 1943-45, because repatriation and POW files are held separately from ordinary service files and asking for both by name saves a second letter. A South African service file gives date and place of birth, next of kin, and the addresses given on enlistment and discharge — WHICH BEARS DIRECTLY ON THE 1948 QUESTION, because it would place him, or fail to, in the year that matters.

rows.what: The Catholic marriage register at Rosebank, 7 September 1940 — Archdiocese of Johannesburg
rows.note: The civil registers have no parents' columns. Catholic sacramental registers do. Leonard and Phyllis were married at Rosebank by W. P. Whelan, who filled in the Denomination line himself as "Catholic Priest", and they were married BY BANNS rather than on a licence — so the intention was read in church on three Sundays and generates its own entry as well. A parish marriage register of 1940 ordinarily names the father and mother of both parties. This is a church record, so it sits entirely outside the Home Affairs eligibility problem in request 15. Identify the Rosebank parish in the Archdiocese of Johannesburg and write to it. SENT as request 17. The parish is the Church of the Immaculate Conception, 16 Keyes Avenue, Rosebank, established 1936 — four years before the wedding. Not asserted as certain: the civil register gives only the word Rosebank, so the letter asks to be redirected if the marriage belongs to another parish or to a chaplaincy at the Roberts Heights camp. Both letters disclose plainly that David is not a descendant and makes no claim to be. SENT 15 September to Info@rosebankcatholicchurch.co.za, Gmail 1a0a3b72c965ecf1.

rows.what: Leonard's own birth certificate, GRO, Hitchin, first quarter 1917
rows.note: THE OBVIOUS DOCUMENT THIS ARCHIVE HAS NEVER ORDERED, and it should be embarrassing that it took until now. Every route tried this week has been an attempt to get Leonard's parents out of a SOUTH AFRICAN record — marriage registers with no parents' columns, an estate that does not exist, a military file, a parish book. His ENGLISH BIRTH CERTIFICATE names his father and mother outright. The index entry is already held: WEAR, Leonard A R, Hitchin, Q1 1917. A GRO certificate costs about GBP 12.50 and arrives as a PDF in days. If it names Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle, the single weakest link in the whole chain — that Leonard is their son, currently resting on a seven-person family tree built by his daughter — becomes a government record. A purchase, so David's, but this is the cheapest decisive document on the entire list. || REFERENCE PINNED 16 September from FreeBMD, so the certificate cannot be ordered wrong: HITCHIN, March quarter 1917, vol 3a page 1244 — WEAR, Leonard A R, mother CASTLE. The birth certificate names the father and gives his occupation and the family's address at the time.

rows.what: The Wear-Castle marriage certificate, GRO, Hitchin, fourth quarter 1914
rows.note: The companion to the row above, and the generation behind it. The archive established that the ONLY Wear-Castle marriage in the whole English index is Henry R Wear to Martha L Castle, Hitchin Q4 1914. The certificate names BOTH FATHERS, with their occupations. That does two things at once: it confirms the couple from a state record rather than an inference, and it pushes the line back a generation on both sides at a stroke. Same cost, same speed. || REFERENCE PINNED 16 September from FreeBMD, so the certificate cannot be ordered wrong: HITCHIN, December quarter 1914, vol 3a page 1552 — WEAR, Henry R, spouse CASTLE. The 1914 certificate names the fathers of BOTH parties — Henry Robert Wear's father and Martha Maud Castle's father on one sheet — so it pushes this line back a generation in a single document.

rows.what: All six Wear children, from the GRO index on the mother's maiden name
rows.note: DONE — and the row should never have been written. It claimed the sibship had been cited repeatedly while only four of the six were named. That was false: section 7 of the Wear notes names all six with quarter and district, from FindMyPast's England & Wales Births searched on mother's maiden name CASTLE — six results, all Hitchin. Leonard A R Q1 1917, Janette E M Q4 1919, Kathleen E Q1 1921, Cynthia Y E Q2 1931, Linda A Q2 1933, Bruce W Q3 1936. Closed with the reason attached rather than deleted: the work list exists to stop the archive re-doing work, and a row written without re-reading the notes does the opposite.

rows.what: Name the second son, and find out what became of him
rows.note: DONE, and it produced the most important thing on the list. The second son was already named — BRUCE WALLACE WEAR, Q3 1936 Hitchin, in South Africa by 1959, four marriages and three divorces in the Witwatersrand. What was NOT known is whether he is dead. The notes said "Bruce was gone by 2014", inferred from his wife Edwina's estate notice naming no surviving spouse. Tested against two indexes on 15 September: the Verified Death Database holds Edwina and NOT Bruce; the Government Gazette estate notices hold Edwina and NOT Bruce. And the inference has an obvious alternative — he had already divorced three wives, so a fourth divorce leaves her with no surviving spouse while he lives. Absence is not proof of life and he could have died abroad. But the honest position is now 'not recorded as dead in South Africa', not 'gone by 2014'. See row 31: born 1936 he would be ninety, and he is not a cousin — he is LEONARD'S BROTHER, a direct male-line son of Henry Robert Wear.

rows.what: Is there a living male-line Wear who could take a Y test?
rows.note: SHARPENED 15 September, and it now has a name. The candidate is not a distant cousin to be hunted: it is BRUCE WALLACE WEAR, Leonard's younger brother, born Q3 1936, who carries the same Y chromosome the archive is trying to match against Derrick's R-S11477. Row 30 establishes that he is not recorded as dead in South Africa. If he is living he is ninety. ONE Y-37 test from him confirms or destroys this entire investigation in a single reading, for a fraction of the Big Y in row 14. He is a living person: nothing about him goes on the site beyond the index entry already published, and THIS ARCHIVE WILL NOT APPROACH HIM. Whether anybody does is David's, and it walks straight into row 15. *** THREE NAMED CANDIDATES, 17 SEPTEMBER, and they come from the 1881 census rather than from hope. *** Robert Wear had three brothers in his father's house at Jamaica Road in 1871 — WILLIAM b.1850, JAMES b.1852 and HENRY b.1854, all three harness makers at their father's trade. JAMES IS STILL IN JAMAICA ROAD TEN YEARS LATER: RG11 piece 574, folio 56, page 8, schedule 501, 42 JAMAICA ROAD, BERMONDSEY — James Wear, 29, harness maker, born WALWORTH; wife Ann; Gertrude 7; AND TWO SONS, LOUIS b.1878 AND HARRY b.1881. A SECOND HOUSEHOLD a few streets off at 2 FENNER ROAD, RG11/567/128/60 schedule 1238, has WILLIAM WEAR, 38, SADDLER — his father's exact trade, the same parish, the same sub-district — with a son WILLIAM b.1875. THAT ONE IS PROBABLE AND NOT PROVED AND THE FILE SAYS SO: the age gives 1843, which is five to seven years out against both the 1851 and the 1871 returns, and the birthplace column is blank. SO THE Y-CARRYING CANDIDATES ARE LOUIS WEAR b.1878, HARRY WEAR b.1881 and — IF THE FENNER ROAD MAN IS OURS — WILLIAM WEAR b.1875. Three boys, all Bermondsey, all in the male line from William Wear the saddler of Walworth. AND THIS IS THE ONLY ROUTE LEFT ON THIS SIDE. Henry Robert's own siblings cannot do it: LOUISA'S ONLY CHILD DIED IN THE QUARTER HE WAS BORN, Rosetta never married, and the two Hull half-siblings share Emma Hawkins but not Robert Wear. NEXT: follow Louis and Harry to 1891, 1901, 1911, 1921 and 1939, then to marriages and sons; and search the match list for the surname WEAR against the twelve-region Wear signature, which a Jamaica Road cousin should hit and a Castle cousin should not. *** FOLLOWED THE SAME AFTERNOON, AND THE TRAIL BREAKS — SAID PLAINLY RATHER THAN LEFT HOPEFUL. *** The death index for ST OLAVE SOUTHWARK gives the next chapter: ROBERT WEAR b.1859 died Q1 1890, and WILLIAM JOHN WEAR b.1849 DIED Q2 1890 — TWO OF THE BROTHERS INSIDE TWO QUARTERS, at thirty-one and forty-one, and the second entry hands us a middle name the censuses never gave. ANN MARIA WEAR b.1852 died Q1 1895; two Wear children, ALBERT GEORGE b.1886 and PHOEBE b.1890, died in 1891. BUT NEITHER LOUIS NOR HARRY IS IN THE 1911 CENSUS OR THE 1939 REGISTER under that name, and the 1891 census shows why the search is hard rather than why they are gone: EIGHTEEN WEARS IN BERMONDSEY IN 1891, and their birth counties are MIDDLESEX AND LANCASHIRE, not Surrey. Even the James Wear of 1891 was born in Middlesex; ours was born at Walworth. BERMONDSEY IS TO WEAR WHAT BALDOCK IS TO CASTLE. The brothers cannot be followed on a name from here, and the next step is not another index search — it is the ST OLAVE SOUTHWARK BAPTISM AND BURIAL REGISTERS, which name parents on every line, or the 1891 household pages read one by one for a Surrey-born James.

rows.what: The 1953 Salkow marriage register, read at full resolution
rows.note: DONE 15 September. Certificate 146 of 1953, Johannesburg, frame 1087, image 3:1:3Q9M-CSV4-R9JG-K, rebuilt from 336 tiles. Morris Isaac Salkow, 31, born Transvaal, DIVORCEE, salesman. Ivone Luwinski formerly de Witt born de Figueredo, 25, Portuguese East Africa, DIVORCEE, SALESLADY, of 9 Rudney Road, Rossmore. rows.what: Find a South African marriage form that DOES have a parents' column
rows.note: ANSWERED, and the answer is NO. The South African civil marriage register never asked for parents — not in any decade and not on either form. The archive had read five (1940, 1948, 1951, 1952 eleven-column; 1956 on the fourteen-field B.M.D. 3(a)). A genuine 1970 register was pulled and read to test whether a later redesign added them: image 3:1:3QS7-L9Z5-GQPP, entry no. 2 of 1970, form B.M.D. 3. Its fourteen fields are names, date, solemnized at, identity number, race, age and date of birth, ante-nuptial contract, personal status, occupation, place of birth, address, banns or licence, consent, remarks. Not one is a parent. The state asked more and more about the parties themselves and never once asked whose children they were.

rows.what: Gillian's 1969 marriage register, Heather's 1968, Patricia's 1997
rows.note: STRUCK by row 33 the same evening it was proposed. rows.what: Re-read the 1952 Halsey-Wear register for the columns nobody looked at
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and it paid. The sheet had been opened once, for column 4, which redirected the whole archive; nobody went back for the rest. (2) Banns, at St Martin's-in-the-Veld, denomination ANGLICAN CHURCH — so the Wears were Anglican, and the 1940 Catholic ceremony came from Phyllis's side, which is what request 17 guessed and now has evidence for. And one disappointment worth recording: column 9, Consent given by, reads 'Own' for both — had Cynthia been a minor it would have carried her father's name outright.

rows.what: Estate-notice sweep: Martha Maud Wear 1986, and every Wear estate 1965-1990
rows.note: DONE 15 September by driving NAAIRS itself rather than a mirror of it. THE SWEEP FOUND NO WEAR ESTATE IN THE TRANSVAAL BETWEEN 1970 AND 1976; the last is the father's, MHG 10245/69, remarks SURVIVING SPOUSE MARTHA MAUD WEAR. Martha Maud's own 1986 estate is NOT absent — it is out of range, because the deceased-estate index runs to the end of 1976 and stops (2,246 estate records in 1976, one in 1977, zero after). That has to be got from the Master's office direct, which is row 2's correspondence. The measurement is the real result: it makes Leonard's two published death years asymmetric for the first time — 1973 is INSIDE the index and he is not in it; 1979 is three years past its last year and cannot be tested at all. Published on /leonard/ with the limits stated.

rows.what: Sweep the Government Gazette for Leonard the engineer
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and closed for a structural reason worth stating. Every exact form returns zero — "Wear, Leonard Aubrey Robert", "WEAR, L. A. R.", "L A R Wear" — and every loose form is useless: Wear+engineer+Johannesburg returns 5,568 documents and Wear+Fairlands+Johannesburg returns 3,469, because WEAR IS AN ORDINARY ENGLISH WORD appearing in trade names (More Wear Industries, Fashion Wear, Boys' Wear Manufacturing), wool-labelling prosecutions and railway reports about flange wear. THIS IS THE EXACT OPPOSITE OF THE LUWINSKI CASE AND THE ASYMMETRY MATTERS: Luwinski is rare, returns eight hits in the whole archive, all read, so a null means something. Wear returns thousands, none of them people, so a null means nothing. The archive will stop treating the two nulls as the same kind of object.

rows.what: Kurt's naturalisation, and a plain answer about whether such lists exist at all
rows.note: DONE 15 September, both halves, and the plain answer is YES THE LISTS EXIST AND NO KURT IS NOT IN THEM. The Government Gazette publishes naturalisation in two series — intention-to-apply notices under section 10 of the South African Citizenship Act 1949, and lists of certificates actually issued; 246 gazettes carry the heading and both were read in full for 1975 and 1976 while working row 58. A full-text search of every South African gazette returns LUWINSKI exactly eight times and this archive had already read all eight — six Piccadilly Hat Company partnership notices, the 1972 Paula application and the 1975 Pallou's Dress Centre notice. NONE IS A NATURALISATION NOTICE. Luwinski is a rare surname and the same search demonstrably finds him, so unlike the WEAR null this one is worth something. NAAIRS cannot help: a search of the central-government database for NATURALIZATION returns 342 documents and every one is a POLICY FILE OR A BILL — the 1926 Act, its 1927 amendment, South West Africa bills. Individual naturalisation files are not indexed at item level anywhere this archive can reach, so the remaining route is a letter, which is row 61.

rows.what: Sweep CASTLE through the South African record the way WEAR was swept
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and it returned a coincidence that has to be handled rather than filed. TAB WLD 155/1915 and 329/1919: DIVORCE, MAUD MABEL LONGHURST (BORN CASTLE) VERSUS AUBREY LEONARD — the index writes the defendant by forenames alone because the surname is shared, and TAB MHG 3632/50 gives him in full as AUBREY LEONARD LONGHURST, died 1950, second wife Athalie born van Aardt. SO: A WOMAN CALLED MAUD, BORN CASTLE, MARRIED TO A MAN CALLED AUBREY LEONARD, IN JOHANNESBURG, TWO YEARS BEFORE LEONARD AUBREY ROBERT WEAR WAS BORN TO MARTHA MAUD CASTLE. Three elements of this archive's central identity in one line. It is probably nothing: Martha Maud was nineteen in 1915, married in Hertfordshire since 1914 and on the 1921 census at Letchworth, so she is not the plaintiff, and both Castle and Maud are common. BUT IT WOULD ANSWER A QUESTION NOBODY HERE HAS ASKED OUT LOUD — WHY JOHANNESBURG? Emigrating families go where somebody already is, and if Maud Mabel Castle was Martha Maud's aunt or elder cousin then the Castle family had a Johannesburg branch twenty years before the Wears arrived, and a boy christened Leonard Aubrey in 1917 was named after his mother's relative's husband. NOTHING IS CLAIMED. Written up in castle-baldock.md with the caution attached, because a later reader who found these three references without it could do real damage. Also swept: WEAR+CASTLE returns zero across all repositories — no South African record joins the two names.

rows.what: Leonard's grave — and with it, probably, the death year
rows.note: WORKED and came back empty, which is itself worth having. Searched the FamilySearch collection that holds both his parents — South Africa, Gauteng, Johannesburg, Cemetery Records 1840-2019 — plus every South African death, burial and Find a Grave collection. LEONARD AUBREY ROBERT WEAR APPEARS EXACTLY TWICE IN ALL OF FAMILYSEARCH'S SOUTH AFRICAN HOLDINGS: his 1940 marriage and his 1951 marriage. No death, no burial, no grave. That is a real negative rather than a gap in the index, because the same collections hold Henry Robert at West Park in 1969, Martha Maud in 1986, Edwina in 2014 and Michelle in 2017. The likeliest reading is that he did not die in Johannesburg — he was divorced twice and could have gone anywhere. Which points straight back at row 10: GenDatabase's PLACE OF DEATH field is paywalled, and the R20 report would say which province to search. Blocked on that purchase, which is David's.

rows.what: Put Leonard at an address in every year the record allows
rows.note: WORKED to the end of what can be done from here, and the answer is that he cannot be placed. Three addresses in fifty-eight years: 72 Pix Road Letchworth in 1921, Roberts Heights Pretoria in September 1940, Polana Court Abel Road Berea in October 1951. BETWEEN 1941 AND 1950 THERE IS NOTHING AT ALL — no address, one recorded fact, that a daughter was born in 1941 — and 1948 sits in the middle of that hole. Nothing places Leonard in Johannesburg in 1948 except that he married there in 1940 and again in 1951, which is an inference from either side of a gap. The gazette route is now exhausted: full-text searches for Polana Court, Dunottar Street, Abel Road and Greenfield Road against the surname return nothing, and the only two hits for Greenfield Road and Wear are advertisements for ladies' wear. What is left — street and telephone directories, the Deeds Office property index, the voters rolls — all need somebody physically in Johannesburg or Pretoria, and none of them costs a fee worth arguing about. Added to the held brief for the researcher. Published on /leonard/ with the silences given the same weight as the entries. SUPERSEDED IN PART the same evening: a fourth address and a fourth fixed point — 271 Wilson Street, Fairlands, 13 September 1969, from the West Park grave register, folio W 8. Leonard was alive and in Johannesburg on that date, which is the last certain sighting the archive has of him.

rows.what: Date the emigration exactly, from the outward passenger lists
rows.note: Row 12 is marked done, and it is done only in the sense that the emigration is BOUNDED — after the 1921 census, before 29 September 1939. The UK outward passenger lists, BT27, would give the actual ship and the actual date. Two notes have carried this as a to-do for days without anyone touching it. It also answers something the archive has never asked: did Leonard travel WITH his parents, or separately, and at what age. || BLOCKED 16 September: THE FAMILYSEARCH SESSION HAS SIGNED OUT and this row cannot move without it. The catalogue and persona APIs now return 401 and the site redirects to the login page. This archive will not enter credentials on David's behalf. One sign-in in the browser unblocks this row, rows 42, 60 and 88 together, and the post-1970 marriage register test in row 81. || NARROWED 16 September WITHOUT A PASSENGER LIST, and closed at that. NO WEAR MARRIED A FOOT IN ENGLAND AND WALES BETWEEN 1938 AND 1955 — and GenDatabase has Kathleen Edith Wear marrying James Cecil Foot in 1945, so SHE WAS IN SOUTH AFRICA BY THEN. Put with the rest, the window closes hard: Q3 1936 Bruce born at Hitchin, family still in England; 29 September 1939 the household ABSENT from the 1939 Register; Q4 1939 Janette marries Edward Bailey AT HITCHIN, having stayed for the wedding; 7 September 1940 Leonard marries at Rosebank, Johannesburg; 1945 Kathleen marries, not in England. THE HOUSEHOLD LEFT BETWEEN AUTUMN 1936 AND SEPTEMBER 1939, AND TWO OF THE SIX CHILDREN FOLLOWED SEPARATELY. That is a three-year window fixed by records rather than inferred from silence, and it is as far as this goes without the outward passenger lists, which are behind a paywall.

rows.what: Sort every match in the cluster into Wear side, Castle side, or neither
rows.note: DONE 15 September, by ratio rather than by segments, and the limits are published with it. For each shared match, cM-with-Derrick divided by cM-with-Penelope-Browne measures how much of that person's relationship to Derrick is left unexplained by the documented Castle line. All ten shared matches ranked. THE CLOSEST MATCH 3.62, THE 96 cM MATCH 3.32, a 92 cM match 1.96, a 70 cM match 0.97, then the Castle-side core at 0.10 to 0.42. The 96 cM match is in neither of the tables the archive built on 14 September: 96.0 cM with Derrick and only 28.9 with the Castle descendant. On the reasoning that found the Wear line, that is what a Wear-side cousin looks like. Caveats stated on the page: the ratio conflates 'not on Browne's line' with 'distant from Browne', and the denominator is inflated at the bottom because those five are Browne's own first cousins. The bottom of the table is nearly meaningless; the top is not.

rows.what: Triangulate the 253 cM that are NOT Castle
rows.note: DONE 16 September — not by getting the 96 cM match's eight segments, which are still behind the chromosome browser's Advanced panel, BUT BY BUILDING THE THING THAT WILL TEST THEM IN SECONDS WHEN THEY ARRIVE. The archive's argument has always been made by EXCLUSION: these regions are the ones the Castle cousins do NOT share. That is almost impossible to test a new match against, because it asks the reader to hold twelve absences in mind. So it was computed the other way round from the local segment data and written down as coordinates. Subtracting every region either documented Castle-side cousin shares, from the closest match's twelve segments, leaves 253.2 cM IN 12 NAMED REGIONS, now published on /dna/ and stored as data/wear-signature.json. THE COMPUTATION VALIDATES ITSELF: it reproduces this archive's previously published 44.3 cM shared and 253.2 cM not shared TO THE DECIMAL, from an independent method. It also produced the Castle side positively for the first time — the two Castle cousins overlap each other by about 151 cM across nine regions on chromosomes 1, 2, 5, 6, 12 and 18, which is what a tight documented pair should look like, while the closest match overlaps them by only 44. STATED LIMIT: the subtraction is on physical coordinates with cM apportioned by length, and cM and base pairs do not scale together, so the last digit should not be over-read.

Anyone who sees it understands the argument in five seconds. Anyone who reads the prose has to take it on trust. rows.what: Re-verify every address in SHARED-CONTACTS.md, and do it before writing, not after
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the old rule is replaced rather than reaffirmed. All twenty-six addresses this project has used were re-resolved and audited against the six that have actually failed. MX CAUGHT ONE OF THE SIX. The reason is now understood and published: dac.gov.za and dsac.gov.za resolve to the SAME mail gateway, so a renamed department keeps a perfectly valid MX record and the rejection happens inside, where DNS cannot see it. A live MX proves a mail server answers for the domain and nothing about the department, the office or the person. The replacement procedure, ordered by what actually catches things: search the sent mail first for prior contact AND prior bounces (three catches so far); prefer an address the institution itself gave you over a directory entry; check the institution still exists under that name and at that address; MX last, for a mistyped subdomain; then watch a day for a bounce. Written into SHARED-CONTACTS.md in both archives and published on /letters/.

rows.what: The Momple and Robertson line, so that Phyllis stops being a name
rows.note: BROKEN OPEN 15 September, after sitting untouched because Momple was a name with nothing attached. One NAAIRS query attached a family. TAB WLD 3046/1959: DIVORCE, LOUIS JAMES MOMPLE ROBERTSON VERSUS FLORENCE PERTHINIA — A JOHANNESBURG MAN CARRYING MOMPLE AS A MIDDLE NAME AND ROBERTSON AS A SURNAME, which is the classic signature of a mother's maiden name carried forward and exactly the joint this archive needed, since Phyllis Agnes ROBERTSON's mother was a MOMPLE. He is very probably her brother or first cousin. And behind him a whole family with estates: MHG 6060/50 MOMPLE, LOUIS ARTHUR, surviving spouse DORA MOMPLE BORN CARLSE; MHG 695/64 Dora Momple; TPD 1468/1950 Douglas Arthur Momple in re the late Louis Arthur Momple; and three daughters married out as Archer, Ackhurst and Gervais. MHG 6060/50 IS INSIDE THE ESTATE INDEX'S RANGE AND CAN BE ORDERED — its death notice names Louis Arthur Momple's parents and its estate file lists his children. If Phyllis's mother is among them, row 52 is answered and the Mauritian line behind her opens with it. || REASSIGNED 16 September. Everything reachable from a desk has been done: the family is identified, the surname joint is found, and the estates are located. WHAT IS LEFT IS AN ORDER, NOT A SEARCH — MHG 6060/50, Louis Arthur Momple, died 1950, surviving spouse Dora born Carlse. rows.what: John Anderson Wear, buried at West Park — who is he?
rows.note: STRUCK within the hour, and it is worth saying why. The Find a Grave record's PLACE field offers five candidate cemeteries for the ambiguous string 'West Park Cemetery' — Johannesburg, Cleveland Ohio, Long Eaton Derbyshire, Hereford Texas, and Bulawayo — and FamilySearch surfaced the Johannesburg one only because the query was filtered to South Africa. The record's own Country, State, County and City fields resolve to UNITED STATES OF AMERICA / TEXAS / DEAF SMITH / HEREFORD. He also appears as a father in Illinois births of 1883. He is an American and has nothing to do with this family. A place-name collision in an index, caught before anything was published — which is the first time this week that has happened before rather than after.

rows.what: 64 Greenfield Road, Greenside — find out who lived there
rows.note: DONE 15 September — overtaken rather than answered, and the detour was worth more than the row. The gazette gives nothing for 64 Greenfield Road, so instead of hunting the address the CEMETERY REGISTERS were opened, on the reasoning that a burial register records where the dead lived and a grave register records who BOUGHT the grave. Both are true. West Park Cemetery Private Graves Register, folio W 8 (published here first as W58; corrected the same evening): purchaser WEAR, Mr L. A. R., of 271 WILSON STREET, FAIRLANDS, receipt 11484, 13 September 1969, sixty pounds, grave 56045 section E.C., person buried HENRY ROBERT WEAR. Read at five times magnification the initial is a cursive L, not a J. And the 1986 burial register gives Martha Maud, aged 90, died at the Hillcrest Geriatric Centre, usual residence 12 and a half Second Street, PARKHURST — buried in grave 56045, the same grave. Row 55's own question is still unanswered; it has been overtaken, because the archive now has an address for LEONARD, which is what it actually wanted.

rows.what: Who authorised the second burial in grave 56045 in 1986
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is that THE RECORD WAS NEVER MADE. Four more West Park images were rebuilt tile by tile. (1) The full two-page spread of Martha Maud's 1986 burial, folio W 104, image 3:1:3QHV-B3PY-2FKN, 7,407 x 3,164, 377 tiles: cause NATURAL CAUSES, burial order 37640, 17.3.86, undertaker REG, receipt 61610, R70.00, nature of interment "New Reopen." — and the Remarks column, which is where an authority would be noted, is EMPTY for her row. Not illegible, not cropped: empty. (2) The index side of the Private Graves folio, image 3:1:3QHV-13P1-89VT, read line by line across three magnified passes, holds exactly ONE Wear: Henry Robert, 13.9.69, grave 5604/5, Fol. W56. MARTHA MAUD IS NOT IN IT. A 1986 interment into a 1969 private grave generated no new private-grave entry, which is itself the explanation for the blank Remarks column: the reopening was handled as a burial, not as a grave transaction, so nobody had to sign for it. The row closes with the reason attached, not struck. What is left is the undertaker's own file — the register names REG — or Martha Maud's estate at the Master of the High Court, and neither is worth a row until the Master answers what it already has. THE DETOUR PAID AGAIN, twice: burial register folio W 56 row 4 gives HENRY ROBERT WEAR's usual residence, 5 LIVINGSTONE CT., 4TH ST., PARKHURST — the first address ever recorded for him in South Africa — with address at time of death General Hospital Jhb., died 11.9.69 of BRONCHOPNEUMONIA aged 80, burial order 2894, undertaker Cooks, R15.00. And the folio number this archive published for the grave register was WRONG: it is W 8, not W58, confirmed three ways.

rows.what: 5 Livingstone Court, 4th Street, Parkhurst — run the parents' documented address
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and it paid far beyond the address. One gazette query on "Livingstone Court" returned four South African hits; the 1965 and 1977 ones are other people, but GOVERNMENT GAZETTE 4620 OF 21 MARCH 1975, under NATURALIZATION NOTICES, carries: EVANS, Mrs Janette Eileen Maud, formerly Bailey, nee WEAR, saleslady, 5 LIVINGSTONE COURT, 28 VIERDE STRAAT/FOURTH STREET, PARKHURST, JOHANNESBURG. The OCR interleaves two columns and the entry had to be unpicked from its neighbour, so the page itself was read. And the grant followed in GAZETTE 5007 OF 12 MARCH 1976: R54033 - EVANS, Janette Eileen Maud, 28/10/19, England, Citizen of the U.K. and C., 30/10/75. THREE GAINS. (1) The Parkhurst address is corroborated from a wholly independent source six years later, with the building's street number added — the cemetery clerk's hand and the Government Printer's type agree. (2) The birth date 28 October 1919 falls inside GRO quarter Q4 1919, so the Hitchin birth and the Johannesburg naturalisation are the same woman without an assumption. (3) THE FAMILY STAYED BRITISH: Leonard's eldest sister was still a citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies in 1975, forty years after the household left Hertfordshire. That explains why a man in Johannesburg from the late 1930s to 1969 leaves so little in South African government series. Also new: she was married twice, formerly BAILEY. Checked and rejected along the way: "Wear, Martha" in Gazette 2438 of 20 June 1969 is MARTHA CUMMINGS WEAR, BORN CAMASK, of 17 Botha Avenue, Witbank, estate 6167/66 — not Martha Maud born Castle. Opened rather than trusted, which is now the rule.

rows.what: 271 Wilson Street, Fairlands — establish whether Leonard owned or rented it
rows.note: NEW, and it follows from the parents being at a DIFFERENT address on the same day. On 13 September 1969 Henry Robert Wear's household was a Parkhurst flat and L. A. R. Wear's was 271 Wilson Street, Fairlands. So the Fairlands address is Leonard's own, not a borrowed family one — which makes it worth testing in a way a family address would not be. A Deeds Office search on the erf will say whether he held title, and if he did it will say when he bought and WHEN HE SOLD OR DIED OUT OF IT, which bears directly on 1973 against 1979. Costs a search fee and needs somebody in Johannesburg; add to the held researcher brief rather than opening a correspondence. || REASSIGNED 16 September: this was never a desk job and should not have sat under "this archive". A Deeds Office search on the erf needs a person in Johannesburg. It belongs with REQUEST 14's Deeds Registry question, which already asks about the ante-nuptial contracts, rather than standing alone.

rows.what: Folio F 3/8 — the possible transfer of the grave rights
rows.note: NEW and deliberately small. Row 4 of burial folio W 56 carries two lines in its Remarks column: "P. Fol. W.8.", which is the private-graves cross-reference and is certainly Wear's, and above it, in a smaller darker hand, "Transf. P.Fol. F 3/8." — a transfer of private rights to or from folio F 3/8. The ruling below both lines puts them in row 4's cell, but the page curves across two thousand pixels and the upper line may belong to row 3. THE ARCHIVE IS NOT CLAIMING IT. If it does belong to Wear then the grave rights in 56045 were transferred, and whoever they were transferred to is a name this archive does not have — which is the question row 57 asked and could not answer from the books it opened. Resolving it means finding the F-series folio in the same film and reading what grave it covers. rows.what: Naturalisation file R54033, and whether Leonard ever had one
rows.note: NEW, and it is a record class this archive has never used. A gazette naturalisation notice is a name and an address; the FILE behind it records date and place of birth, previous nationality and PARENTS. Row 33 established that the South African civil marriage registers have no parentage field at all — this series does. Certificate R54033 was granted to Janette Eileen Maud Evans, nee Wear, on 30 October 1975; if the file names Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle it is the first South African government record to state that couple as the parents of a child. It does not prove Leonard was theirs. THE SECOND QUESTION IS THE BIGGER ONE: ask in the same letter whether any naturalisation file exists for WEAR, Leonard Aubrey Robert, born 1917. A phrase search of the gazette returns nothing for him and no Wear in either the 1975 notice list or the 1976 grant list, but the lists are alphabetical and the OCR interleaves columns badly enough that this very entry had to be unpicked by hand — SO THAT NULL IS NOT AN ANSWER. Files for this period sit with the Department of Home Affairs, older series transferred to the National Archives, Pretoria. A letter, not a purchase. Send with the Master of the High Court business. || WORKED 16 September to the point of deciding WHO to ask, and the answer is nobody new. NAAIRS does not index individual naturalisation files — its 342 NATURALIZATION documents are policy files and bills — so the file behind certificate R54033 sits with the Department of Home Affairs or in an unindexed National Archives series. THE ARCHIVE ALREADY HAS TWO LIVE THREADS THAT COULD CARRY THE QUESTION: Enquiries2@dsac.gov.za, which answered within two days on 12-14 September, and Ms Mavis Xaba at mavisx@dsac.gov.za, WHO HAS ALREADY BEEN WRITTEN TO TWICE AND MUST NOT GET A THIRD COLD THREAD. So this is not a new letter: it is one added question on the existing NARS thread, asking whether naturalisation files of the 1970s are held by them or by Home Affairs, and whether the file behind a known certificate number can be produced. Cheap, and it avoids the duplication this archive has already been burned by once.

rows.what: The Bailey marriage — Janette Wear married twice
rows.note: DONE 16 September, AND IT IS THE BEST THING FOUND THIS WEEK. The archive did not know which country the Bailey marriage was in, let alone which year. It is the FIRST of the thirty-six, and it is ENGLAND. FreeBMD, Marriages, December quarter 1939, >99% complete: WEAR, Jeanette E M — spouse BAILEY — HITCHIN — vol 3a page 4416; and the reverse, BAILEY, EDWARD J — spouse WEAR — same volume and page. HITCHIN IS THE FAMILY'S OWN REGISTRATION DISTRICT, where all six Wear children were born. TWO CONSEQUENCES. First, it rewrites the 1939 Register. That register, taken 29 SEPTEMBER 1939, found her alone at 18 Ridge Avenue, Letchworth, and this archive read it as "and one daughter stayed" — the household gone to South Africa, a girl of twenty left behind. SHE WAS NOT LEFT BEHIND; SHE WAS STAYING TO BE MARRIED, within three months and probably less. Second, and this is the point: AN ENGLISH MARRIAGE CERTIFICATE NAMES BOTH FATHERS. Row 33 established that the South African register has no parents' column at all — which is why the whole sibship rests on a seven-person family tree, why request 19 goes to the Master for three estates, and why row 61 chases a naturalisation file. This certificate costs about £14 and comes by email.

rows.what: WLD 978/1960 — who was Mawthane Dabeah Kwele, and why was he suing Leonard

rows.what: Ivone's naturalisation — the one route that names her parents on a South African form
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is a bounded negative that is itself a fact about her. The gazette was swept YEAR BY YEAR 1946-1980 for the forename Ivone — the search API takes a year filter and pages, which is how a common forename becomes tractable. Ten South African gazettes carry it in that window and EVERY ONE WAS OPENED: a Radium Station general dealer in 1951, Ivone da Conceicao Isaac in the 1962 grant list, Maria Ivone Freitas Basilio de Abreu of Emmarentia in 1967, Ivone Bertholet de Oliveira e Sousa Duran of Lourenco Marques in 1968, Maria Ivone Silva Almeida in the 1968 grant list, Maria Ivone Melo Gouveia in the 1970 list. NONE IS HER. The exact forms "Salkow, Ivone", "Ivone Salkow", "LUWINSKI, Ivone", "MOTA FIGUEIREDO" and "Rocha, Ivone" return zero each. IVONE DID NOT NATURALISE AS A SOUTH AFRICAN under any of her three surnames. The sweep also taught the format — surname, forenames, date of birth, country of birth, previous nationality, certificate number — and showed the lists FULL of Portuguese and Madeiran names through exactly the years she lived there. Other Portuguese naturalised steadily; she did not. That fits a woman who went back to Portugal and died at Porto, and it makes the Portuguese correspondence more important, not less.

rows.what: Martha Maud Wear's 1986 estate — outside the index, so it must be asked for

rows.what: The England and Wales probate calendar, 1970–1990, for Leonard
rows.note: WORKED 15 September to the end of what is free, and the result is a second instrument on which 1973 fails. The England and Wales probate service is free and its images ARE viewable without an account — but IT DOES NOT NAME-INDEX ANYTHING BEFORE 1996. A surname-and-year search returns scanned calendar pages and matches the string anywhere on the page, so WEAR also catches Weardale and Wearmouth. Searched with the keyword AUBREY to cut the noise: 1973 returns ZERO PAGES; then 8, 24, 19, 31, 13, 23, 19, 13 for 1974 to 1981. THE FAMILY TREE'S YEAR RETURNS NOTHING, on a second independent index, the evening after the South African estate index said the same. The 1979 pages have NOT been read — twenty-three dense calendar pages is an afternoon by eye, or minutes on a commercial index that has keyed the calendar by person. The row stays open and now says what it would cost. || CLOSED 16 September by row 73 rather than by reading the images. If he did not die in England or Wales between 1970 and 1985 — and a 99%-complete index that prints dates of birth says he did not — then there is no English death for an English grant of probate to follow. The 23 unread pages for 1979 would be a search for something now known not to be there. ONE CAVEAT KEPT, because it is real: an English grant CAN follow a foreign death, and the calendar records those in a recognisable form — a page read on the way records ADAMSON, Charles Mary, "of 126 The Gardens Esplanade Durban SOUTH AFRICA died 7 April 1979 administration with will Pietermaritzburg £3500 in England and Wales SEALED London 3 December 1981". So a resealed South African grant would appear. That is a narrower search than the one this row began with, and it is the only reason not to mark the row struck.

rows.what: GRO consular and overseas death registrations for Leonard
rows.note: STRUCK 16 September — not abandoned, but CLOSED STRUCTURALLY, and it is worth more struck than it was open. Row 73 promoted this to the most important untested thing about him. It turns out the series CANNOT CONTAIN HIM, for three separate reasons carrying three different weights. (1) FIRM: the GRO consular death registers run 1849 TO 1965, and both candidate years are outside them. (2) FIRM, from gov.uk itself: the modern statutory service covers deaths "on or after 1 JANUARY 1983" and is optional — 1973 and 1979 are both before it. (3) PROBABLE BUT NOT PROVEN, and marked as such because it is a council web page and not legislation: Coventry City Council's guidance lists SOUTH AFRICA among countries where a death CANNOT be registered with the British authorities at all, alongside Australia, Canada, Bermuda and Zimbabwe — which is what one would expect of Commonwealth countries with their own civil registration. ANY ONE OF THE THREE WOULD BE ENOUGH; ALL THREE AGREE.

rows.what: The GRO death index for England and Wales — in case he went home
rows.note: DONE 16 September, and it is THE BEST-BOUNDED NEGATIVE THIS ARCHIVE HAS EVER PRODUCED ON HIM. Row 58's finding that the family stayed British raised a hypothesis nobody had entertained — that Leonard went home to die. HE DID NOT. FreeBMD transcribes the GRO index; its coverage chart for deaths shows EVERY QUARTER FROM 1970 TO 1983 AT 100%, and the search prints the figure beside each quarter: 58 CONSECUTIVE QUARTERS, EVERY ONE MARKED >99%. And from 1969 the GRO death index carries FULL FORENAMES AND THE DATE OF BIRTH, so he can hide behind neither an initial nor a common surname. Searched WEAR, deaths, March 1970 to December 1985, no forename: 241 ENTRIES, SIXTEEN OF THEM BORN 1915-1919, AND NOT ONE IS HIM. The only 1917 birth is a Sam Wear of Halifax. A separate search on the forename Leonard returns exactly one man, Leonard Rigby Wear born 10 October 1897, died Claro June 1970 — twenty years too old, wrong county. SETTLED: he did not die in England or Wales between 1970 and 1985, in either candidate year or any year between.

rows.what: Sweep every surname in the archive through NAAIRS, now that it can be driven
rows.note: DONE 16 September, and it paid for itself on the fourth surname. THE FIND IS WLD 2225/1953: ILLIQUID CASE. DIVORCE. MORRIS ISAAC SALKOW VERSUS IVONNE (BORN DE FIGUERIDO). THEY MARRIED ON 13 FEBRUARY 1953 AND HE SUED HER FOR DIVORCE IN THE SAME YEAR. The archive knew the marriage ended — FamilySearch has him marrying in 1943, 1953 and 1960 — but not that it ended almost at once; Johannesburg case numbers ran to five figures by the 1970s, so 2225 of 1953 is not a December filing. Three consequences: it removes a stepfather the archive had been assuming was a constant through Derrick's childhood; it explains the hole after 1953 as a fact about her life rather than a failure of searching; and it is a new orderable document naming Ivone, whose summons would recite the date and place of the marriage, both ages and domiciles, and the children by name. ALSO SWEPT: NORQUOY gave Robert Selwyn (row 82); MOMPLE gave the Robertson joint (row 39); CASTLE gave the Longhurst coincidence; SALKOW gave nine Johannesburg estates all inside the index window, one of which is probably Morris Isaac's parent; and LEIBHOLZ returns ZERO across all repositories, which is expected — they were never in South Africa — and is recorded so nobody runs it again.

rows.what: The PIO immigration-papers series — Kurt's arrival, and everyone else's
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is that KURT'S ARRIVAL IS NOT IN THE INDEX AT ALL. The PIO immigration series is real and indexed at item level, and it holds exactly one Wear and no Luwinski. rows.what: Every WEAR burial at West Park, not just the two this archive stumbled on
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the answer is that LEONARD IS NOT THERE. Searched by collection rather than by guesswork — f.collectionId=4453927, the Johannesburg cemetery registers, 517 raw hits on the surname, collapsed to six distinct people: HENRIETTA WEAR buried 1909, HENRY ROBERT WEAR 13.9.1969, MARTHA MAUD WEAR 19.3.1986, EDWINA ANN WEAR 8.7.2014, MICHELLE ANN WEAR born 1978 died 27.3.2017, and DAN B WEAR undated. TWO WEARS ARE NEW: Michelle Ann Wear, born 1978, the right age to be a granddaughter of Bruce Wallace Wear who married four times; and Dan B Wear. Both written down, neither pursued.

rows.what: Grave 56045 — is there a stone, and what is carved on it
rows.note: Two people are in that grave and a third person paid sixty pounds for it. A private grave of 1969 in section E.C. would ordinarily carry a memorial, and the burial register has a Remarks column headed "Private Rights, MEMORIALS" in which other rows on the same page record memorials erected and their cost. A photograph of the stone would say who is commemorated and, if a family stone, possibly who paid for it and when it was last added to. Ask the City of Johannesburg cemeteries office, or any of the local volunteer photographers who work West Park. Costs nothing but a request.

rows.what: The undertakers — Cooks in 1969 and REG in 1986
rows.owner: the City of Johannesburg / the firms
rows.note: WORKED 16 September to the limit of what can be established from here, and it is LESS TRACTABLE THAN IT LOOKED. "COOKS" is a specific firm named against Henry Robert Wear in September 1969 and nothing else on that page. "REG", which the 1986 register gives for Martha Maud, IS ALMOST CERTAINLY NOT A FIRM AT ALL — it appears against most rows on the 1969 page as well, which is not how an undertaker's name behaves. It is far likelier to be a clerk's abbreviation, and the archive WILL NOT GUESS WHICH: reading it as a company and writing to that company would be the Caroline Walls error again. Doves, founded 1882 and headquartered in Johannesburg, is the obvious large survivor and could be asked, but there is no evidence connecting it to either entry. WHAT THIS ROW ACTUALLY NEEDS IS THE REGISTER'S OWN KEY — the abbreviation table a cemetery clerk would have used — or one question to the City of Johannesburg cemeteries office, which is the same office row 78 must approach for the photograph of grave 56045. rows.what: Phyllis Agnes Robertson — the Norquoy marriage of 14 June 1952, and what became of her
rows.note: ADVANCED 15 September — a candidate name, from NAAIRS. Phyllis remarried a Norquoy on 14 June 1952 and Leonard sued "Phyllis Agnes Norquoy" in 1957. NAAIRS holds fourteen Norquoy documents and two are a Johannesburg man in exactly the right years: WLD 1198/1957, Edward William Allen versus ROBERT SELWYN NORQUOY, and TPD 1624/1960, Sadi Jacobs versus Robert Selwyn Norquoy. ROBERT SELWYN NORQUOY IS VERY PROBABLY HER SECOND HUSBAND — rare Orkney surname, right city, right decade, and WLD 1198/1957 filed the same year as Leonard's WLD 790/1957 against her. Stated as an inference from surname, place and date; no document yet joins them. Next: the 1952 marriage register under the name Norquoy, and his estate. There is no Norquoy estate for a Phyllis Agnes in the index, but the index stops in 1976 and she may have outlived it. || BLOCKED 16 September, and the blocking is specific. She is NOT in the South African death databases under NORQUOY — thirty-one Norquoy records and not a Phyllis among them — so either she died elsewhere, or remarried again, or the index does not have her. The remaining free route is her 1952 marriage register: South African civil marriages are on FamilySearch to 1974, so a June 1952 Johannesburg marriage SHOULD be reachable — but the FamilySearch session has signed out and this archive will not enter credentials. rows.what: Marjorie Eileen Walker, formerly Dunlop — Leonard's second wife
rows.note: DONE 16 September, end to end, and she turns out to be the best-recorded person in Leonard's orbit. MARJORIE EILEEN WALKER, born 1916, died 2003. THREE HUSBANDS AND SIX COURT FILES: WLD 185/1949, divorce, Marjorie Eileen DUNLOP (born Walker) versus Robert John; then 30 October 1951, marries LEONARD at Polana Court, Abel Road, Berea; then WLD 2960/1962 divorcing Leonard and WLD 2961/1962 suing another woman for damages one number later; then WLD 2276/1973 and WLD 7613/1973, Roger William Hannay HUMPHREY against her; then death in 2003 as MARJORIE EILEEN HUMPHREY, BORN WALKER, WITH AN ESTATE FILE. TWO THINGS THIS CHANGES. First, she divorced Dunlop in 1949 and married Leonard in 1951, and Leonard's own divorce is WLD 2026/1951 — two people coming out of two marriages within two years of each other. 1948 sits immediately before her divorce, and the archive's blank nine years for Leonard end exactly where her paper trail begins. Second, and this is the point: SHE WAS MARRIED TO HIM FOR ELEVEN YEARS, THE LONGEST DOCUMENTED RELATIONSHIP OF HIS LIFE, AND HER 2003 ESTATE CARRIES A NEXT-OF-KIN AND HEIRS SCHEDULE THAT LISTS HER CHILDREN.

rows.what: What happened to the Piccadilly Hat Company after 1952
rows.note: DONE 15 September, and the shop had a life before Kurt. The 1940 page was unreadable in OCR, so the PDF page was rendered at 200 dpi and read as an image. Government Gazette 2825 of 8 November 1940, page VII: NOTICE OF SALE OF BUSINESS — "The business of PICCADILLY HAT SHOP carried on by PICCADILLY DRESS SALOON (PROPRIETARY), LIMITED, at HANNAH COURT, 81 ELOFF STREET, Johannesburg, has been sold and will be transferred to IVY FUCHS, a public trader, who will carry on the said business under the same style or firm at the same address for her own account and benefit as from the 1st of October, 1940." Attorney Israel Katz, Sauer's Buildings. THREE GAINS: the building is named — HANNAH COURT, which this archive did not have; the shop belonged to a company, PICCADILLY DRESS SALOON (PTY) LTD; and KURT BOUGHT IT FROM A NAMED PREDECESSOR, IVY FUCHS, who had held it for thirteen months. He bought a going concern with a history, not an empty name. Also found: 16 May 1952 no. 4846 lists "Piccadilly Hat Co." in a registration schedule under VCR. 429/8/49, a 1949 registration.

rows.what: Write to the Portuguese matches about Ivone's parents
rows.note: DRAFTED as REQUEST 23, HELD — these go to living private individuals and only David can send them, which row 6 already establishes. THE CASE FOR THEM IS THE STRONGEST THING IN THE AUTOCLUSTERS REPORT. Four of the twenty clusters are Portuguese — fifteen people, about 776 cM — and because Derrick's mother was Portuguese from Lourenço Marques, EVERY ONE OF THEM IS ON HER SIDE. Three separate clusters means three separate ancestral couples, which is what a Figueiredo–Mota marriage plus their own parents' lines should look like; one is probably the MOTA line and another the FIGUEIREDO. THE SCALE, PLAINLY: the strongest shares 133.2 cM, MORE THAN ANYONE THIS ARCHIVE HAS EVER WRITTEN TO ABOUT IVONE, and more than the letters to Lisbon, Maputo and Porto have produced between them. The letters are in Portuguese with English below, sent through MyHeritage's own messaging because the export gives tree links and not addresses. ONE MESSAGE PER CLUSTER, to the strongest member, saying openly that one or two others in the same group are being written to — NOT all fifteen, who may well know each other and would read fifteen near-identical messages as harvesting. Order: the 133.2 cM cluster, then the one with two over 100, then the one whose members share an 8,911-person tree, then the weakest only if the others produce nothing. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT: anything about the paternity question. It is Derrick's private business, it concerns his FATHER's side, and it has no bearing on what a Portuguese cousin can help with. The maternal line is not in doubt, and a stranger told a delicate thing in a first message usually stops replying. The ask is one question — do the names MOTA, FIGUEIREDO or PINTO DA ROCHA appear in your family, and is there any link to Mozambique — with an explicit statement that no money or estate is involved. THE FIRST USEFUL ANSWER IS A PLACE: a parish or district in Portugal. With a parish the Portuguese civil registers become searchable and row 65's dead end reopens at no cost.
