rows.what: /tree/ moved onto the shared five-word evidence ladder — and one claim demoted for it
rows.note: DONE 16 September. The tree page had four hand-rolled marks — proved, inferred, unknown, excluded — invented that morning. The sibling archives share a FIVE-WORD LADDER in @daviddef/archive-kit: DOCUMENTED, a record was read and it says this; PROBABLE, the evidence points one way and nothing points the other; INFERRED, reasoned from what is known and not witnessed in a record; FAMILY, told or written on somebody's chart and not sourced; DISPUTED, two sources disagree and neither has been ruled out. The page now uses the shared component, so a level means the same thing wherever a reader meets it. TWO OF THE OLD FOUR WERE NEVER EVIDENCE GRADES AND ARE NOT FORCED ONTO THE LADDER. 'Unknown' is the ABSENCE of a claim; 'excluded' is a claim TESTED AND FAILED. Both keep their own chips, drawn deliberately unlike the ladder — no fill, dashed edge — so they cannot be mistaken for a grade, and the legend says in capitals that they are not levels. AND THE EXERCISE COST ONE CLAIM, WHICH IS THE REAL VALUE OF IT. GEORGE WILLIAM CASTLE AND CAROLINE WALLIS WERE MARKED PROVED AND ARE NOW MARKED PROBABLE. The marriage, the nine children and the dates came from another researcher's tree, not from records this archive has read. What IS documented, because the 1871 census was pulled and read here, is that a George Castle, 30, agricultural labourer, was at Norton End as SON-IN-LAW to James Giddins with a son George, 8. What is NOT is the birthplace at Willian, the October 1882 marriage and the nine children. THE CENSUS ALSO DISAGREES WITH THAT TREE TWICE — it gives the boy's birthplace as BALDOCK, not Willian, and his birth year as 1863, not 1862. Under the ladder that is exactly what PROBABLE means. The marriage certificate, already on the list, would settle it.

rows.what: JANETTE STAYED — the 1939 Register finds her in Letchworth lodgings seven weeks after her mother sailed
rows.note: DONE 16 September on the Findmypast subscription. The 1939 Register was taken on 29 SEPTEMBER 1939, seven weeks after the Dunvegan Castle left London — so it catches exactly the people who did not go. SEARCHED WEAR AT LETCHWORTH: ONE RESULT, AND IT IS HER. TNA R39/1620/1620C/004/42, 18 RIDGE AVENUE, LETCHWORTH, schedule 279: LOUISA CORBY b. 14 Jan 1870, single, unpaid domestic duties; LOTTIE CORBY b. 3 Mar 1881, single, hand sewer; and JEANNETT (E M) WEAR, B. 28 OCTOBER 1919, SINGLE, CINEMA CASHIER. AN EXACT DATE OF BIRTH WHERE THIS ARCHIVE HAD ONLY 'JANETTE 1919'. AND SHE IS NOT WITH FAMILY. She is nineteen, lodging with two spinster sisters, and working in a cinema. Her mother and the four youngest had sailed for Durban on 10 August; her father had gone in April. SHE STAYED, WITH A JOB AND A ROOM. Note also RIDGE AVENUE against the 9 RIDGE ROAD where her father boarded in 1911 — the same corner of the same small town, twenty-eight years apart. LEONARD IS NOT IN THE REGISTER AT LETCHWORTH OR HITCHIN, which is consistent with his having already gone, BUT IT IS NOT PROOF: the register's own notice says officially closed records are withheld for people not proven dead, and LEONARD'S DEATH YEAR IS PRECISELY WHAT THIS ARCHIVE CANNOT SETTLE — 1973 or 1979. If the National Archives does not know he died, his entry would be closed and would look exactly like absence. A search on WEAR born 1916-1918 returns 61 people and none is a Leonard. Saved to data/wear-1939-register.tsv.

rows.what: CORPORAL L A R WEAR, 141272 — a prisoner of war, and the reason for the silent decade
rows.note: SURFACED 16 September against the BT 27 transcript of Leonard's 1937 crossing and not yet read. FOUR RECORDS: L A R WEAR, GERMANY 1939; and L A R WEAR, GREAT BRITAIN, 1943, 1944 and 1945. TREAT THEM AS A PROBLEM BEFORE TREATING THEM AS A LEAD. A man who sailed from Southampton to the Cape in March 1937 and married at Rosebank, Johannesburg, in September 1940 is not obviously in GERMANY IN 1939, and the 1943-45 Great Britain records sit oddly against a life this archive believes was lived in Johannesburg. THREE READINGS, AND THEY ARE NOT EQUALLY LIKELY. (a) THEY ARE A DIFFERENT L A R WEAR — the initials are not rare and Findmypast's suggestions match on name alone, which is exactly how the Giddins error happened this afternoon. (b) THEY ARE HIM, AND HE CAME BACK — possible, and it would mean the 1937 emigration was not permanent. (c) THE 'GERMANY 1939' RECORD IS A PRISONER-OF-WAR OR CASUALTY INDEX whose date is the campaign rather than the man. WHAT TO DO: open each one and read the service number, the unit and any date of birth BEFORE deciding it is him. If any carries a birth date matching Q1 1917 at Hitchin, that settles it. THIS ALSO BEARS ON ROW 25, the SANDF service record, which assumes he served South African. *** READ 16 SEPTEMBER, AND THEY ARE HIM. *** The row said to treat them as a problem before a lead and to read the service number before deciding anything. THE SERVICE NUMBER IS WHAT DECIDED IT. All five records carry 141272; the rank is CORPORAL; and the force is not a British regiment but the SOUTH AFRICA UNION DEFENCE FORCES. TNA WO 392/15 and WO 392/21, the War Office Directorate of Prisoners of War lists for 1943-1945. HE WAS A PRISONER OF WAR, HELD IN GERMANY, listed in 1943, 1944 and 1945. THE 'GERMANY 1939' TAG THAT LOOKED SO WRONG IS THE CAMP, NOT A POSTING, and the 1939 is the collection's war-span label rather than a date. THE SOUTH AFRICAN FORCE IS WHAT TURNS INITIALS INTO A PERSON. Leonard sailed for the Cape in March 1937, married at Rosebank in September 1940, and was twenty-five when Tobruk fell in June 1942 and something over ten thousand South Africans were taken prisoner in a day. AND IT EXPLAINS THE SILENCE THIS ARCHIVE HAS BEEN RECORDING FOR WEEKS. Row 41: Leonard cannot be placed between 1941 and 1950 — no address, one recorded fact, a daughter born in 1941. A MAN IN A PRISON CAMP DOES NOT APPEAR IN A DIRECTORY, ON A VOTERS' ROLL OR IN A NEWSPAPER. The hole is not an absence of records; it is an absence of liberty. HELD AS PROBABLE, NOT DOCUMENTED: the lists give INITIALS ONLY AND NO DATE OF BIRTH, so the case rests on initials, force, a fitting age, and one number repeating across five records in two volumes. WHAT SETTLES IT IS THE SANDF SERVICE RECORD AT PRETORIA — row 25, wanted since the archive began and never askable precisely. IT CAN NOW BE ASKED FOR BY NUMBER.

rows.what: Follow-up to SANDF with the force number
rows.note: DRAFTED 16 September, NOT SENT. A FOLLOW-UP INSIDE THE EXISTING THREAD 1a0a3b70c6389154, not a new letter — the Centre already has the 15 September enquiry and a second approach would be the scattering Ms Xaba complained of, in a different inbox. WHAT MAKES IT WORTH SENDING IS THAT IT REMOVES WORK RATHER THAN ADDING IT. The original letter asked, at question 3, whether the medal rolls might yield a force number, and said in as many words that WITH A NUMBER THE REST BECOMES ORDINARY. The number is now in hand: 141272, Corporal, South Africa Union Defence Forces, prisoner of war in Germany, from TNA WO 392/15 and WO 392/21. SO QUESTIONS 3, 4 AND 5 OF THE ORIGINAL ARE WITHDRAWN — no medal-roll search, no nominal index needed. THE CAVEAT IS STATED RATHER THAN BURIED: the POW lists carry initials only and no date of birth, so the identification rests on initials, the South African force, a fitting age and one number repeating across five records. The letter says plainly that 141272 may belong to somebody else and that being told so would be a useful answer. FOUR ASKS: the attestation or personnel record for 141272; whatever it gives for PARENTS OR NEXT OF KIN, which is still the heart of it because South African marriage registers of the period have no parents' column and an attestation form does; the PRISONER-OF-WAR AND REPATRIATION PAPERS, which are sometimes filed separately and are worth asking for now rather than in a second exchange; and THE ADDRESSES GIVEN ON ENLISTMENT AND DISCHARGE, because a discharge address is the first thing that would place him after the war and 1948 is the year that matters. *** SENT 16 SEPTEMBER 2026, message 1a0aa27caa5e8b60, inside the existing thread 1a0a3b70c6389154. *** The chase clock on that thread is reset to a fortnight. IF THEY ANSWER AT ALL, THE ATTESTATION FORM IS THE MOST IMPORTANT SINGLE DOCUMENT THIS ARCHIVE HAS EVER ASKED ANYBODY FOR: the entire Wear chain rests on Leonard being a son of Henry Robert Wear and Martha Maud Castle, and the only source that says so is a seven-person tree built by his own daughter. An attestation form naming his parents would turn that into a government record.

rows.what: TAB MHG 7584/69 — KURT'S OWN ESTATE, and it is not on the researcher's list
rows.note: FOUND MISSING 16 September while going deep on Kurt at David's instruction, AND IT IS THE MOST SERIOUS OMISSION ON THE PRETORIA LIST. Twenty-six references went to the researcher this afternoon — seven Booyzen, seven Wear and Luwinski court files, five Lerena, and the six already agreed — AND KURT'S OWN ESTATE FILE IS NOT AMONG THEM. It has been in this archive's own records for days: ZA TAB MHG_#_7584/69, LUWINSKI, KURT, the estate opened after he died at Johannesburg on 15 December 1968. WHY IT MAY BE THE MOST IMPORTANT MHG FILE IN THE WHOLE ARCHIVE. A South African death notice, form J294, asks THREE things this archive wants and cannot otherwise get. (1) THE DECEASED'S PARENTS. Kurt's father was JACOB LEIBHOLZ, deported to Auschwitz in February 1943, and his mother AUGUSTE LUWINSKI — who did not marry until January 1924, TWELVE YEARS AFTER KURT WAS BORN, which is why he stayed a Luwinski while his younger brother was registered a Leibholz. THE ARCHIVE ASSERTS THAT PARENTAGE FROM GERMAN SOURCES AND HAS NO SOUTH AFRICAN DOCUMENT FOR IT. The J294 would be one, signed by whoever buried him. (2) HIS PLACE OF BIRTH, which would test the East Prussian story against a form filled in by his family rather than by him. (3) AND THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST: THE LIST OF SURVIVING CHILDREN. Derrick was legally Kurt's son and was about twenty when Kurt died. WHETHER THE DEATH NOTICE NAMES HIM — AND HOW — IS A FACT ABOUT WHAT THE FAMILY BELIEVED AND RECORDED IN 1968, twenty years after the marriage that produced him and fifty-eight before the DNA said otherwise. EITHER ANSWER IS WORTH HAVING. HOW IT SHOULD GO, AND NOT BY A THIRD EMAIL TODAY. The researcher has just been sent a long list and told to cut from the bottom; a separate message adding a twenty-seventh item would be exactly the scattering Ms Xaba complained of, in another inbox. SHE HAS NOT YET SENT THE INVOICE, so there will be a natural reply. IT RIDES ON THAT ONE, and it should be marked as belonging near the TOP, not the bottom.

rows.what: How Kurt actually got to South Africa — not through Britain, so the lists are Hamburg's
rows.note: TESTED AND ELIMINATED 16 September, and the elimination is the useful part. Kurt arrived in South Africa in 1933, a German Jew of twenty-one leaving the year Hitler took power, and THIS ARCHIVE HAS NEVER ESTABLISHED HOW HE TRAVELLED. The obvious test was BT 27, the British outbound passenger lists, because a great many refugees went out through Southampton. SEARCHED ON LUWINSK* ACROSS THE WHOLE SERIES 1890-1960: SIX RESULTS, ALL ONE POLISH FAMILY OF LUWINSKAS SAILING LIVERPOOL TO PORTLAND, MAINE, IN 1908. He is not in it. SO HE DID NOT LEAVE FROM A BRITISH PORT, and the record of his crossing is not at Kew. THAT POINTS SOMEWHERE SPECIFIC: the HAMBURGER PASSAGIERLISTEN, the Hamburg passenger lists, which run to 1934 and are held at the Staatsarchiv Hamburg — or the Bremen lists, most of which were destroyed. A Hamburg entry would give his age, his last residence, his occupation and his destination port IN HIS OWN EMIGRATION YEAR, which is the one document that would show what he left with and what he called himself. NOT REACHABLE FROM THE CURRENT SUBSCRIPTIONS: the Hamburg lists are indexed on Ancestry, which is signed in but not subscribed, and at the Staatsarchiv direct. A single pay-per-view or a trial month would cover it, which is the same narrow case already recorded for the WWI pension records.

rows.what: Pauline had two husbands before Kurt — two new court files
rows.note: FOUND 16 September going deep on Kurt. His last wife PAULINE, born RAPPOPORT 1914, died 1985, is carried in the register as 'Pauline Rappoport / Miller (Luwinski)' and nobody had asked what the Miller was. THERE ARE TWO EARLIER MARRIAGES AND BOTH ENDED IN COURT. TAB WLD 583/1944 — ILLIQUID CASE, DIVORCE, PAULINE MILLER (BORN RAPPOPORT) VERSUS JOSEPH. TAB WLD 332/1952 — ILLIQUID CASE, DIVORCE, PAULINE BERMAN (FORMERLY MILLER, BORN RAPPOPORT) VERSUS ISRAEL. So she married JOSEPH MILLER, divorced him in 1944, married an ISRAEL BERMAN, divorced him in 1952, and married Kurt after that. BOTH REFERENCES ARE NEW TO THIS ARCHIVE and are added to litigation.tsv. AND IT COMPLETES A PATTERN NOBODY HAD NAMED. Kurt married at least three times and EVERY WIFE HAD BEEN MARRIED BEFORE: Ivone was a de Witt when he married her in June 1948 and had been married four months; Frances Hostowsky appears in the records as Hostowsky Berner Sefton Luwinski, which is three surnames before his; and Pauline arrived with two divorces behind her. A man who married three much-divorced women in a decade in one city is a fact about the man, not just about them. PRIORITY LOW AS FILES — they are Pauline's marriages, not Kurt's, and neither would name his parents — but they belong on any future Pretoria list and they are cheap to add to one.

rows.what: No gazette notice for Kurt's estate, which is itself odd
rows.note: NOTICED 16 September while looking for the executor of MHG 7584/69. South African deceased estates are ADVERTISED IN THE GOVERNMENT GAZETTE — this archive has used exactly those notices to find the Wear estates at Cape Town and the two Figueiredo estates — and the notice names the executor and gives an address for claims. KURT DIED ON 15 DECEMBER 1968 AND HIS ESTATE IS MHG 7584/69, SO A NOTICE SHOULD APPEAR IN 1969 OR 1970. SEARCHED THE GAZETTE FOR LUWINSKI AND LUWINSKY ACROSS 1968 TO 1972: ONE HIT ONLY, and it is the 1972 sequestration brought by Paula Luwinski. NOTHING FOR KURT AT ALL. THREE READINGS AND THE ARCHIVE SHOULD NOT PICK ONE YET. (a) The OCR lost it — entirely possible on these scans, and this archive has already seen 'Figueiredo' rendered as 'Epo .Figueiredo,CarlosDe'. (b) The estate was small enough to be wound up without the advertisement that larger estates require. (c) The notice ran under a spelling nobody has tried. WHAT IT MEANS PRACTICALLY: the cheap route to Kurt's executor is closed, and MHG 7584/69 itself — already raised as the most serious omission from the Pretoria list — becomes the only way to the death notice and the children it names.

rows.what: Tell the second-cousin match that the Martha Giddings line in my letter was wrong
rows.note: RAISED 16 September. The reply sent to him this afternoon contains one sentence that later research contradicts: 'If Martha Giddings died in 1863 she cannot have known her son at all, and I notice your George William is with his grandparents in both 1871 and 1881.' THE DEATH INDEX WAS THEN FOUND — third quarter 1863, Hitchin, volume 3A page 188 — AND HIS BAPTISM IS 4 JANUARY 1863. She lived at least six months past it; the boy was about a year old. SHE KNEW HIM. WHAT TO SAY AND WHAT NOT TO. It is one sentence in a long letter, it was offered as an observation about HIS tree rather than a claim about mine, and he has given no sign of caring either way. IT DOES NOT WARRANT AN EMAIL OF ITS OWN — a correspondent who sends a second message to amend a subordinate clause is a correspondent people stop answering. IT GOES IN THE NEXT REPLY, briefly, with the volume and page so he can check it, AND WITH THE PART THAT IS BETTER THAN AN APOLOGY: the finding itself is new to both trees, and it is his ancestor as much as ours. *** DRAFTED 17 SEPTEMBER, NOT SENT: requests/27-SEND-THIS-to-paul-correction.txt. *** It leads with the correction rather than burying it. THE ERROR: 'If Martha Giddings died in 1863 she cannot have known her son at all' — she died in the THIRD QUARTER of 1863 and he was baptised on 4 JANUARY of it, so she had him for something under a year. Both numbers were already on file and the quarters were never compared. IT ALSO CHANGES THE READING OF THE 1871 CENSUS, which the letter says: the widower is IN the house at Norton End, enumerated son-in-law with his boy as grandson, so he did not give the child away — he went to his dead wife's parents and was still there eight years later, and those two relationship words are the census's own and are now the proof of the line. A second caution goes with it: the same census gives the boy's birthplace as BALDOCK not Willian and his birth year as 1863 not 1862, and the letter says so rather than quietly amending his tree. THEN THREE THINGS THAT ARE HIS, not ours: CAROLINE REMARRIED — Q3 1920 Hitchin, Caroline Castle to JAMES JAMES — and was CAROLINE JAMES when she died in 1957, which is the whole reason his great-grandmother cannot be followed past 1916; her exact date of birth is 28 FEBRUARY 1863 from the 1939 Register at 38 Norton Road, not the 1862 every tree carries; and the surname is WALLIS not Walls, six GRO birth entries to none. It closes with Pix Road, flagged as not his line but worth having. Offers images of everything.

rows.what: EMMA REMARRIED — she became Emma Hull, and the whole household is found in 1901
rows.note: FOUND 17 September, and it closes three separate questions at once. EMMA HAWKINS, WIDOWED AT THIRTY-TWO IN 1891, HAD NEVER BEEN FOLLOWED PAST THAT CENSUS. Three direct tests failed: no Emma Wear in Hertfordshire in the 1901 census, no remarriage indexed under Emma Wear, no death. SHE WAS SEARCHED FOR UNDER THE WRONG SURNAME. Coming at it through the children found her at once. 22 MOUNT PLEASANT, ST ALBANS — 1901 census, RG13/1312: JOHN HULL, head, 33, RAILWAY LABOURER; EMMA HULL, wife, 41, BORN ALDENHAM — which is what identifies her, since Aldenham is a small parish and it is her birthplace in both the 1861 and 1871 returns. With ALBERT J HULL aged 6 and EDITH M HULL aged 4, both born St Albans; and LOUISA S A WEAR 18, ROSETTA E WEAR 15, AND HENRY R WEAR 11, ALL ENTERED AS STEP-CHILDREN OF JOHN HULL. WHAT IT SETTLES. (1) Emma remarried about 1893-94 and had two more children. Henry Robert was raised from about four by a stepfather who was a railway labourer. (2) ROSETTA WAS ALIVE AT FIFTEEN and is an APPRENTICE STRAW HAT MAKER — the Hertfordshire county trade, the same industry in which her step-grandmother Elizabeth Giddins was doing 'platting' at Norton End in 1871. She had simply been searched for under Wear in the wrong decades. (3) LOUISA IS CONFIRMED AS LOUISA S A WEAR, which is exactly the form that married a SHENTON at Hitchin in 1918. AND IT OPENS SOMETHING NEW AND DNA-RELEVANT: ALBERT J HULL b.1895 AND EDITH M HULL b.1897 ARE HENRY ROBERT'S HALF-SIBLINGS. Their descendants would share with Derrick THROUGH EMMA HAWKINS ONLY — not through Robert Wear and not through the Castles — which isolates the Hawkins line by itself. No match on the current list carries Hull.

rows.what: 63 AND 72 PIX ROAD — Emma Hawkins was alive, blind and on her son's street when the family sailed
rows.note: FOUND 17 September while looking for Louisa's Shenton household, and it is the most striking thing the Findmypast month has produced. TNA R39/1620/1620G/011/28, SCHEDULE 305, 63 PIX ROAD, LETCHWORTH, taken 29 September 1939: EMMA HULL, BORN 7 FEBRUARY 1859, WIDOWED, 'INCAPACITATED - BLIND'; LOUISA SHENTON, born 29 November 1882, married; WILLIAM SHENTON, born December 1876, 'INCAPACITATED'. EMMA HULL IS EMMA HAWKINS. Born at Aldenham, married Robert Wear at Southwark in 1881, widowed in 1890, remarried John Hull about 1893, AND WIDOWED A SECOND TIME BY 1939. At eighty she is blind and living with the daughter who was eight when her father died. HER EXACT DATE OF BIRTH IS NOW KNOWN and it comes from the best kind of source — a woman of eighty giving it to a registrar in person. SO IS LOUISA'S: 29 NOVEMBER 1882. AND THE ADDRESS IS THE FINDING. HENRY ROBERT WEAR AND MARTHA MAUD RAISED SIX CHILDREN AT 72 PIX ROAD. HIS MOTHER AND HIS SISTER WERE AT 63 PIX ROAD. THE SAME STREET, a few doors along, in a garden city of eight thousand that had not existed forty years earlier. IT GIVES THE EMIGRATION A SHAPE IT DID NOT HAVE. Leonard went in March 1937, his father in April 1939, his mother in August with the four youngest — and the register, taken seven weeks after that ship sailed, finds still in Pix Road an eighty-year-old blind woman and the daughter keeping her, with Janette in lodgings half a mile off on Ridge Avenue. THE RECORD SAYS WHO WAS WHERE AND NOTHING ABOUT WHAT ANYBODY FELT, and the page says so. BUT IT IS NO LONGER TRUE THAT THE FAMILY SIMPLY LEFT. Still open: no children are in the Shenton household, so whether Louisa had any — the independent test of the Wear half — is unanswered; she was 57 and any would have gone.

rows.what: AT LEAST TWO CASTLE CHILDREN HAVE NEVER BEEN NAMED — Caroline bore nine and one was already dead in 1911
rows.note: OPENED 17 SEPTEMBER by the fertility question on the 1911 census. RG14/7572, schedule 173, St Mary's Cottages, Baldock: CHILDREN BORN 9, STILL LIVING 8, DIED 1. Against that this archive holds SEVEN names — George William 1884, Ada May 1887, Fredrick James 1889, Agnes Kate 1892, MARTHA MAUD 1895, Florence Margaret H 1901, Ernest Albert C 1904 — of which six came from the GRO birth index searched on the mother's maiden name WALLIS. SO TWO ARE MISSING AND ONE OF THE NINE DIED BEFORE APRIL 1911. WHERE THEY WILL BE: the gaps are 1889-1892 and 1895-1901, and the second gap is six years wide in a family that otherwise produced a child every two or three. HOW TO FIND THEM: re-run the GRO birth index on mother's maiden name across ALL spellings, not only Wallis — Walls, Wallice, Wallace — because the missing two may simply be mis-indexed; then the Baldock burial register for a Castle infant. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND COMPLETENESS: an unidentified son is another chance at a Castle male line, and the only Castle male line this archive has is Frederick James, who has now vanished twice. *** WORKED THE SAME AFTERNOON, AND THE METHOD FAILED IN AN INSTRUCTIVE WAY. *** The plan was to re-run the birth index on every spelling of WALLIS. THAT IS NOT THE PROBLEM. MARTHA MAUD'S OWN BIRTH ENTRY — Q3 1895, Hitchin, volume 3A page 561 — HAS NO MOTHER'S MAIDEN NAME IN THE INDEX AT ALL; THE FIELD IS BLANK. So the search that found six was never going to find nine, whatever it was spelt: it returns the children whose entries happen to carry the field and drops the others in silence, and the woman this archive descends from is one of the ones it drops. A FILTER ON A FIELD THAT IS SOMETIMES EMPTY IS A FILTER ON THE INDEXING, NOT ON THE FAMILY. THE DISTRICT SEARCH DOES NOT RESCUE IT EITHER: Castle births at Hitchin between 1884 and 1906 run to FOUR PAGES, because there are at least three unrelated Castle families in the town. WHAT IS LEFT, AND IT IS THE RIGHT INSTRUMENT ANYWAY: the BAPTISM REGISTER, which names both parents on every line. Martha Maud was baptised at Baldock on 22 September 1895, so the family used it. Findmypast's Hertfordshire Baptisms set has Castles at Baldock back to 1693 and would not take a year filter in the URL, so this needs the search form rather than a crafted address — or the Hertfordshire Archives register itself. THE TWO MISSING CHILDREN ARE STILL MISSING, and the gaps are still 1889-1892 and 1895-1901.

rows.what: FREDERICK JAMES CASTLE IS NOT THE MAN WHO DIED AT HITCHIN IN 1975 — and he is in no English record after 1901
rows.note: THE EXCLUSION IS NOW DOCUMENTED RATHER THAN ASSERTED, 17 September. Frederick James Castle, born 1889 at Hitchin to a mother nee Wallis, is Martha Maud's brother and THE ONLY CASTLE MALE LINE THAT COULD EVER CARRY A Y TEST. The obvious candidate death — FREDERICK JAMES CASTLE, Hitchin, 1975 — BELONGS TO SOMEBODY ELSE. The 1939 Register has that man at 17 ORCHARD ROAD, BALDOCK, BORN 10 APRIL 1887, 'Vertical Driller On Aircraft Work', married to Ella, with a third person in the household whose record is officially closed. Same name, same town, two years out. AND BALDOCK SUPPLIES A THIRD: the 1921 census has an entirely separate Castle household at 5 CEMETERY ROAD — head James Castle, nine children — with its own Frederick, 33 years 2 months, a hydraulic press operator at Letchworth. THREE MEN OF ONE NAME IN ONE SMALL TOWN INSIDE TWO YEARS, which is exactly why name-only identification at Baldock is worthless. WHAT IS LEFT OF OUR MAN: he is in no Hertfordshire census in 1911, in no census in 1921, in no 1939 Register entry, and in NO ENGLISH DEATH INDEX BETWEEN 1889 AND 2007 under any Fred-form of the name. FOUR THINGS COULD EXPLAIN THAT and they are testable: he died in the Great War, at 25 in 1914 (check Soldiers Died and the CWGC register); he emigrated, which this family demonstrably did; he died abroad; or he is the one of the nine who was dead by 1911, in which case the 1889 birth and an infant burial at Baldock should meet. THE FIRST IS THE ONE TO RUN, because a war death would also be a record naming his mother and her address.

rows.what: THE SHENTON LINE IS CLOSED — Louisa had one child and he died in the quarter he was born
rows.note: ANSWERED 17 SEPTEMBER, and the answer is no. The Pix Road find opened one specific question: LOUISA SHENTON WAS HENRY ROBERT WEAR'S SISTER, so a descendant of hers would carry the WEAR half of Derrick's ancestry AND NOT THE CASTLE HALF — the independent test this archive has wanted since the segment reading, and the one thing that could separate the couple. No children were in the 1939 household, and the transcript confirms it held EXACTLY THREE PEOPLE with no officially closed records hidden in it. SO THE INDEXES WERE ASKED DIRECTLY. Births, surname SHENTON, mother's maiden name WEAR: ONE RESULT — STANLEY W SHENTON, Q1 1924, HITCHIN. Deaths, surname Shenton, born 1924: STANLEY W SHENTON, Q1 1924, HITCHIN. BORN AND DIED IN THE SAME QUARTER. His mother was forty-one. AND THE MOTHER'S-MAIDEN-NAME TRAP WAS AVOIDED THIS TIME, because it had just caught this archive over Martha Maud: the district was searched as well, surname SHENTON, HITCHIN, 1916 TO 1936, WITH NO MOTHER'S NAME AT ALL. ONE RESULT. THE SAME ONE. Shenton is a Staffordshire surname and there is exactly one Shenton birth in the whole Hitchin district across twenty-one years. THE MARRIAGE: WILLIAM SHENTON married a WEAR at Hitchin in Q3 1918, when Louisa was thirty-five. THE REST OF THE HOUSEHOLD, now traced end to end: WILLIAM SHENTON, born December 1876, 'Incapacitated' in 1939, DIED Q3 1953 at Hitchin. LOUISE S A SHENTON DIED Q4 1967 AT HITCHIN, AGED 84 — and the initials close it, because her birth is registered as LOUISA SARAH A WEAR. AND THAT BIRTH GIVES A PLACE NOBODY HAD: Q1 1883, KINGSTON, SURREY. Robert Wear and Emma Hawkins married at Southwark in 1881 and their son Henry Robert was born at St Olave Bermondsey in 1889 — IN BETWEEN THEY WERE AT KINGSTON. WHAT THIS COSTS: the Wear half can no longer be tested through Louisa. WHAT IS LEFT: Henry Robert's other siblings, and the two Hull half-siblings ALBERT J b.1895 and EDITH M b.1897, who carry Emma's DNA but not Robert Wear's — which is a different and still useful test, because a Hull cousin should match Derrick on the HAWKINS side ALONE.
